I read both PDFs and inspected the extracted preview in `~/Downloads`. **Your idea fits the track well if the 3D visualization becomes a way to verify answers.** The strongest pitch is: *ask a building a question, and it shows you the exact objects and drawing evidence behind its answer.*

The Stoa challenge, “Make Blueprints Talk,” scores four things equally: answer accuracy, visual verification, creativity, and low inference cost. A beautiful house render helps with creativity; an interactive cutaway that highlights every counted window can address all four.

**What the dataset actually contains**

The preview has **913 drawing/model files across nine sources**, plus **7,990 question–answer records referencing 320 files**. Multiple formats sometimes represent the same drawing.

| Source | Preview contents | Questions | What it offers your project |
|---|---|---:|---|
| CubiCasa5K | 241 PNG floor plans | 4,270 | Image understanding: rooms, doors, windows, fixtures |
| Swiss Dwellings | 65 plans, each in PDF, DXF and PNG | 2,358 | Best starting point for geometry extraction and a 3D floor-plan view |
| IFC models | 4 IFC files, 3 PDFs, 3 SVGs | 1,049 | Existing building geometry and structured properties |
| IFC-Bench | 5 IFC models | 249 | Questions about building properties and semantics |
| Opening Design | 81 PDF/CAD/model files | 64 | Real architectural documentation, schedules and revisions |
| HABS | 92 JPGs | 0 | Historic measured drawings |
| Finna | 96 JPGs | 0 | Finnish archival drawings |
| Europeana | 61 JPGs | 0 | Varied European archival material |
| Wikimedia | 125 JPGs, 7 SVGs | 0 | Diverse floor plans |

The full-dataset README describes roughly 14,000 drawings and 120,000 questions; those figures describe the full release, not this preview.

The preview questions break down into:

- **6,076 counts**
- **1,599 areas**
- **265 text answers**
- **34 volumes**
- **16 lengths**

Counts require exact answers; area, length and volume answers allow a 2% tolerance, according to the README. Many questions are translations of the same task, so 7,990 records do not mean 7,990 independent reasoning problems.

Two particularly useful discoveries:

- A sampled Swiss DXF contains named layers including `WALL`, `WINDOW`, `DOOR`, `ROOM_OUTLINE`, `ROOM_TEXT` and `UNIT_OUTLINE`. That is a promising route to procedural reconstruction, although entities still need interpretation and deduplication.
- **The preview is not consistently a collection of complete buildings.** For example, it contains a rendered FZK house plan without the corresponding house IFC. Some Opening Design files are isolated details or archived revisions, and one IFC is explicitly stored under “bad IFC models.” We should select and validate demo assets deliberately.

There is also a scope trap: one question attached to a fourth-floor PDF asks for doors in the whole model. The system must distinguish “on this sheet,” “on this floor,” and “in this building.”

**How I would shape the idea**

Imagine this interaction:

> “How many windows are on this floor?”

The application answers with a count, highlights numbered windows on the original drawing, and highlights the corresponding objects in an explorable 3D cutaway. Clicking a window opens its source evidence.

For an area question, it highlights the room polygon, displays dimensions or the source quantity, and shows the calculation. This makes the visualization useful to a site engineer.

I would use three input paths:

| Input | Proposed approach | What the visualization can claim |
|---|---|---|
| IFC | Extract elements, properties and geometry | Geometry present in the supplied model |
| DXF / vector plans | Parse geometry and labels; construct a floor model | Measured 2D geometry, with explicitly assumed heights |
| Raster plans | Gemini proposes objects and locations; validate where possible | An inferred reconstruction with visible uncertainty |

A single floor plan usually does not establish roof shape, façade materials or ceiling heights. You can still create a compelling dollhouse view, but any inferred features should be visibly distinguished from documented ones.

**Where Gemini and Blender fit**

Gemini makes sense as the language and visual interpretation layer: understand the question, select relevant evidence, interpret labels, and produce a structured query or extraction. Its API supports both [PDF understanding](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/document-processing) and [structured outputs](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output).

I would have code perform counts and measurements over extracted objects whenever possible. Each answer should retain the selected object IDs and source locations. That gives you reusable evidence and reduces repeated model calls.

For IFC, [IfcOpenShell](https://docs.ifcopenshell.org/ifcopenshell-python/geometry_processing.html) provides a route to processing existing geometry. Preserve element identifiers through conversion so selecting an answer can highlight the same elements in the viewer.

**Blender MCP is worth exploring for scene setup and experimentation.** For the repeatable application pipeline, my recommendation is a controlled Blender Python script with operations such as “load model,” “highlight these IDs,” and “render this camera.” Blender supports [background rendering from the command line](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/advanced/command_line/render.html).

I would keep an interactive browser view for answering questions and use Blender for polished overview shots or cached renders. That avoids making every question wait for a new image.

**Cloud compute: useful, but benchmark the bottleneck first**

Your resources PDF lists:

- **€200 Verda credits** for compute and inference.
- **$100 Modal credits per participant** for CPU/GPU workloads.
- **Gemini API credits**, with no amount shown in the PDF.

Those are the advertised offers in your document; I have not checked redemption conditions or availability.

Cloud rendering is a sensible experiment, especially for polished Blender output. But faster GPUs will not solve incorrect geometry extraction. Measure import, reconstruction, rendering and Gemini latency separately before choosing where to spend credits. Cache geometry and renders so subsequent questions mostly select and highlight existing objects.

**My recommended hackathon scope**

Start with **Swiss Dwellings**, plus **one validated IFC building**:

1. Build a linked drawing and 3D view.
2. Support a small set of questions: room/apartment counts, windows or doors, and room areas.
3. Make every answer highlight its supporting objects.
4. Add Gemini-based image extraction as the ambitious extension.
5. Evaluate on held-out buildings, keeping translations and alternate formats together to prevent leakage. Report accuracy, latency and cost per question.

Keep `questions.jsonl` as evaluation data rather than feeding reference answers into the application. Preserve the attribution from each source’s `LICENSE.md` when displaying drawings.

The key decision is **how much reconstruction you want to own**. I would begin with reliable geometry and build the impressive visual experience around it, then demonstrate reconstruction from a raster plan as an additional capability. That gives you a credible engineering core and still leaves room for the visual impact you’re aiming for.

**You’re right: visual impressiveness should be a core requirement.** My earlier recommendation put too little weight on the experience that gets other hackers to stop, understand the project, and remember it.

I read the new [participant handbook](</home/jcb/Downloads/Junction Platform_particpant_handbook.pdf>). Pages 13–15 confirm:

- Peer review selects the **overall top five**; partners separately select track winners.
- General evaluation covers **innovation, impact, and implementation**.
- Finalists get **three minutes to pitch and three minutes for questions**.
- Submission requires a **public pitch video of at most two minutes**, demo/source links, and a PDF pitch deck.
- The guide lists conflicting peer-review end times: 13:00 in the schedule and 14:00 in the reviewing section. Both start at 10:30.

The handbook doesn’t explicitly score visual polish. Your inference is sensible, though: a striking, understandable demonstration can make innovation and implementation immediately apparent.

**The WAVELET lesson I’d carry over is making an invisible process visible.** For your project, that process is understanding a technical drawing and locating the evidence behind an answer.

I’d shape the experience around this sequence:

| Moment | What the reviewer sees | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|---|
| Open | A dense architectural drawing on a virtual drafting table | The original problem |
| Reveal | The plan rises into an explorable building or floor cutaway | Spatial understanding |
| Ask | “Show me all the windows on this floor” | Natural language interaction |
| Respond | Camera moves; windows illuminate and receive count markers | A useful, visible answer |
| Verify | Clicking a window reveals its location in the original drawing | Evidence and accuracy |
| Follow up | “What’s the area of this room?” highlights its footprint and dimensions | More than a single scripted trick |

**The signature moment should be the drawing becoming a building, followed by the building responding to a question.** That is a compelling visual story even for someone unfamiliar with construction.

I’d make the visual style architectural: clean materials, strong lighting, smooth camera movement, a movable section plane, and animated floor separation. Those features also help users inspect hidden objects. Photorealistic furniture and landscaping would contribute less to this particular demo.

This changes my implementation priorities:

1. **One excellent building experience.** Select a coherent IFC model, inspect its contents, and make navigation, cutaways, highlighting, and source selection feel polished.
2. **A working question-to-object loop.** Gemini interprets the question; code selects and measures objects; the scene animates the result.
3. **A second input example.** Use a Swiss DXF to demonstrate a floor plan becoming a procedural 3D model. Mark assumed heights clearly.
4. **Measured credibility.** Show a small held-out evaluation and actual response costs for Stoa’s accuracy and cost criteria.

There’s an important distinction in the presentation: importing an existing IFC demonstrates model understanding; constructing geometry from a DXF demonstrates reconstruction. Both are valuable, and showing which input produced each scene strengthens the project.

For Blender, I’d now give it a larger role in the visual direction and the pitch video. Cloud rendering could produce an excellent opening shot or transition. **The live question response should still update an interactive scene immediately**, using already loaded geometry. We should benchmark whether Blender itself or a browser viewer gives the smoother live experience before committing.

A possible punchline:

> **“Ask the blueprint. Watch the answer.”**

The first-minute pitch could be: “Finding a simple answer in construction drawings takes far too much searching.” Show the dense sheet, raise it into 3D, ask a question, illuminate the answer, then click through to its source. That connects the spectacle directly to the problem Stoa wants solved.

content.text: alright, lets turn this into a hackathon development plan. This should be narrow, i.e. this is a HACKATHON; i.e. we dont ahve a lot of time and have to focus o the importatn parts, there are two main parts: 1. getting the information required to answer the quetsion reqliably out of the available resoruces and recognize if a answer cant be provided reliably; 2. using the resources availbe to generate a 3d model while aknwoledging invented componetnens and dimensitons since the respective information was not provided.

**Build one complete flow: select a floor plan → ask a question → see a supported answer or an explicit limitation → explore a 3D reconstruction with visible assumptions.**

The two parts should share the same extracted building information. That keeps answers and visualization consistent while preventing invented geometry from becoming evidence.

**Scope the MVP to one input family**

Start with **Swiss Dwellings**, using the matching PDF, DXF and PNG files. We found 65 such sets in the preview, and the sampled DXF has useful named layers.

Use one plan during development and reserve two unseen plans for validation. Support only:

- Room counts, optionally filtered by room type.
- Window counts, if the DXF represents windows consistently.
- Individual room floor areas, where units and closed boundaries can be established.

The reconstruction covers **one floor**, including room footprints, walls and openings. Wall heights, window heights and sill heights can use explicit assumptions. Roofs, furniture, complete-building reconstruction and additional file families are stretch work.

**1. Extract information and decide what can be answered**

Create a small shared building representation. Every room, wall and opening should carry:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Stable ID and object type | Connect answers, drawings and 3D objects |
| Geometry and units | Enable measurements and reconstruction |
| Label or properties | Support questions such as bedroom counts |
| Source reference | Identify the file and CAD entity or drawing region |
| Evidence status per property | Distinguish extracted, calculated, assumed and unknown values |

**Track assumptions per property.** A window’s position can be extracted while its height is assumed. Marking the entire window “verified” would hide that distinction.

The extraction work should establish:

- Coordinate units and scale.
- Room boundaries and labels.
- Window grouping: one window may consist of several drawing entities.
- Wall footprints and openings sufficient for the chosen visualization.

Gemini interprets the question into a small structured request, such as “count windows on this floor” or “calculate area of room R12.” Application code executes that request against the extracted objects. Gemini can also help interpret ambiguous labels, but uncertain interpretations remain recorded.

Use **three answer outcomes**:

| Outcome | When to use it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Supported | Required evidence and checks are present | “This room is 12.4 m²,” with its boundary and calculation |
| Partial | Some relevant information is established | “Eight windows are identified; two symbols remain ambiguous, so the total is unresolved.” |
| Unavailable | A required fact is missing | “Ceiling height is not specified in the supplied files.” |

These outcomes should come from concrete checks, not a model’s self-reported confidence. For example, an area requires known units and a valid closed boundary; a definitive count requires complete coverage of the requested scope and resolved object grouping.

Every supported answer returns the relevant object IDs and source evidence. Keep the supplied answer file out of the answering pipeline; use it only to evaluate results.

**2. Generate a useful 3D model with explicit assumptions**

Generate the model procedurally from the same extracted geometry:

- Extrude wall footprints using a documented height.
- Place room surfaces from their boundaries.
- Position openings from extracted locations and widths where available.
- Apply assumed vertical dimensions where the drawings lack them.

Keep the first version to a clean architectural cutaway with orbit controls, object selection and answer highlighting.

Make assumptions inspectable through a simple **“Show assumptions”** toggle. Selecting a window might show:

> Position: extracted from DXF  
> Width: calculated from source geometry  
> Height: assumed, 1.2 m  
> Sill height: assumed, 0.9 m

Provide one editable assumption initially: **wall height**. Changing it should update the visualization while preserving the answer “actual ceiling height is unknown.” That is a strong demonstration that the system understands the difference between a reconstruction and documented facts.

Use Blender through a repeatable script if it quickly produces the required geometry. Timebox the Blender/MCP/cloud setup experiment to **one hour**. Cloud rendering becomes worthwhile once the actual scene renders correctly; it should not block the question-answering flow.

The visual centerpiece is a smooth **plan-to-3D reveal**, followed by highlighting the objects supporting an answer.

**Build sequence**

These are elapsed milestones for an approximately 20-hour implementation window; adjust for team size and preserve time for the submission.

| Time | Deliverable | Completion check |
|---|---|---|
| Hours 0–2 | Inspect three Swiss plans; choose development and validation files | Confirm units, layer conventions and feasible question types |
| Hours 2–6 | Extract objects, provenance and deterministic queries | A local command answers supported questions and rejects missing information |
| Hours 6–10 | Generate the development plan’s 3D floor model | Footprints align with the source; assumptions are recorded |
| Hours 10–14 | Connect Gemini, answers, source view and 3D selection | Asking a question highlights the same objects in both views |
| Hours 14–17 | Add assumption toggle, height control and reveal animation | A reviewer can understand the workflow without explanation |
| Hours 17–20 | Run held-out checks, fix failures, record demo | Results and limitations are documented; submission assets are ready |

If there are two builders, divide ownership into extraction/answering and reconstruction/interface after agreeing on the shared object format.

**Definition of done**

The demo must demonstrate all four behaviors:

1. **Correct answer:** a supported count highlights every included object.
2. **Traceable measurement:** a room area shows the source boundary and units.
3. **Honest limitation:** an actual-height question is declined when height is absent.
4. **Explicit reconstruction:** changing an assumed height changes the model without turning that assumption into a factual answer.

Evaluate the supported intents on the two held-out plans, plus several deliberately unanswerable questions. Record correctness, refusals, latency and API usage. A small, honest evaluation is enough for this weekend.

If time slips, cut cloud rendering, extra formats and additional question types first. Protect **source-linked answers, reliable refusal, a working 3D cutaway, and visible assumptions**—those are the project.

**Agreed—JPG-only plans belong in the MVP.** That changes the entry point: the system must work from whatever evidence is available, with richer formats improving reliability.

We should build one shared representation that accepts two extraction paths:

- **Image path:** Gemini examines a JPG/PNG or rendered PDF, identifies rooms, walls, openings, labels and dimensions, and returns structured objects with source locations.
- **Structured path:** When a matching DXF or IFC exists, extract its geometry and properties to supplement or check those objects.

For the hackathon, prioritize the image path and add **one** structured adapter—Swiss DXF—once the complete image workflow works.

**Answerability must be decided separately for each question.** A simple JPG might support a bedroom count while providing no basis for floor area or ceiling height.

| Available evidence | Appropriate response |
|---|---|
| Three clearly labeled bedrooms | Answer the count and highlight the three labels/rooms |
| Several clear windows and an ambiguous symbol | Show the identified windows and explain why the total is uncertain |
| Room boundary but no dimensions or scale | Explain that physical area cannot be determined |
| Explicit dimension and a usable boundary | Calculate area only if the geometry and calibration support it |
| No ceiling-height information | State that actual height is unknown; offer a visualization assumption |

Gemini’s confidence score alone should not determine this. Require supporting regions, check for conflicting labels and missing scale, and inspect a relevant crop again when an ambiguity could change the answer. **A second pass can catch mistakes; it does not establish certainty.** We should test this behavior explicitly.

**Separate factual answers from proposals in the interface.**

For example:

> **From your plan:** I cannot determine the ceiling height because no height annotation or section is provided.  
> **For the reconstruction:** I can use an adjustable placeholder height, clearly marked as assumed.

Where an actual comparable example exists:

> **Reference-based proposal:** This reference building specifies height H. We can use that as a starting assumption, but it does not establish the height of your building.

For the hackathon, keep this comparison feature small: a few inspected reference buildings with source-backed properties. Name the reference and explain the relevant similarity. If we have no suitable reference, offer an adjustable default or ask for the missing information. **Visual resemblance alone cannot establish dimensions, structural properties or compliance.**

**The same distinction drives the 3D reconstruction.**

A JPG can produce a useful approximate floor model even without scale:

- Preserve estimated room arrangement and relative proportions.
- Label the model **“Unscaled reconstruction”** until a known dimension is available.
- Mark inferred wall thicknesses, heights and opening dimensions as assumptions.
- Allow the user to supply one known dimension to establish scale, subject to image distortion.
- Highlight uncertain geometry so it can be corrected.

The factual answer engine must never use an assumed reconstruction dimension as source evidence.

**Revised development priority:**

1. **JPG → extracted objects with source regions → supported answer or explicit limitation.**
2. **Extracted objects → approximate 3D floor model with visible assumptions.**
3. **Answer selection → matching highlights in the image and 3D model.**
4. **DXF enrichment → improved geometry and measurements.**
5. **Small reference-based proposal feature**, if time remains.

The demo should include both a sparse JPG and a richer plan. The sparse example proves the central capability: **answer what the drawing supports, explain what is missing, and still produce a useful reconstruction without disguising assumptions as facts.**

Heres some info from a side converstaion: We discussed using the Gemini Decisions API alongside standard Gemini to help the system recognize when construction documents lack enough information to answer a question.

The proposed starting point is one evidence-sufficiency gate: give Decisions the user’s question and actual source material, then classify it as sufficient, insufficient, or unclear. The prompt should allow answers derived through calculation, while checking that essential facts do not need to be assumed. “Insufficient” applies only to the material inspected; “unclear” should trigger further inspection or clarification rather than automatic refusal.

An optional later stage is standard Gemini generates candidate answers and evidence references → Decisions evaluates their support. However, selecting confidently among candidates does not establish that any candidate is correct. Include an unsupported/insufficient option and evaluate against original evidence, not just Gemini’s explanation. Verification should also cover confidently generated answers.

We rejected making many checks independent vetoes: false rejections would accumulate and suppress answer coverage. Start with one overall decision; add targeted checks only for demonstrated failure modes.

Treat confidence scores as signals to validate on this dataset, not guaranteed probabilities of correctness. Compare the gated pipeline against ordinary Gemini using answer coverage and error rate among answered questions, including deliberately incomplete drawings. The goal is fewer unsupported answers without excessive abstention.

I’ll check the Decisions API documentation, then fit a single evidence-sufficiency gate into the plan and define how we’ll test whether it improves reliability.

**Let’s adopt this as the MVP’s single evidence-sufficiency gate.** It fits the reliability goal without expanding the project into a complex verification system.

The revised question-answering flow is:

1. **Collect the evidence:** the question, original drawing, relevant crops, and any available structured geometry. Record exactly which files/pages were inspected.
2. **Make one overall decision:** `sufficient`, `insufficient`, or `unclear`.
3. **Route the result:**

| Decision | Application behavior |

| **Sufficient** | Generate an answer with source references; perform calculations in code where possible. |
| **Insufficient** | Explain what is missing from the inspected material. Offer a clearly labeled reconstruction assumption or sourced comparison where useful. |
| **Unclear** | Inspect a higher-resolution crop, another relevant page, or ask a focused clarification. |

For the hackathon, allow **one automatic follow-up inspection**. If uncertainty remains, explain the unresolved issue and request the missing information. This keeps latency and API usage bounded.

The gate’s instruction should be approximately:

> Determine whether the supplied material supports answering this question without inventing essential facts. Allow calculations when the required inputs, units and geometric relationships are supported. Choose sufficient when the necessary evidence is present and interpretable; insufficient when essential information is absent from the inspected material; unclear when ambiguity, legibility, conflicting evidence or uncertain scope prevents a determination. Typical building dimensions and reconstruction defaults are not evidence about this building.

**A “sufficient” result permits answering; it does not certify the resulting answer.** The generated response must still identify supporting objects or regions. We should retain straightforward calculation and reference checks, and evaluate confidently answered cases alongside uncertain ones. Candidate-answer judging stays an optional later experiment, with an explicit unsupported option.

For the 3D component, the important boundary stays unchanged: **answerability and reconstructability are separate.** Missing height can block a factual height answer while allowing an adjustable, visibly assumed wall extrusion. Neither reconstruction defaults nor similar-building proposals should enter the gate as evidence about the uploaded building.

**Add a small comparison experiment early.** Use roughly 30–40 manually checked question/document pairs covering:

- Clear answers, including answers requiring calculation.
- Missing scale, dimensions or relevant pages.
- Ambiguous symbols and poor legibility.
- Simple questions that remain answerable on sparse JPGs.

Compare ordinary Gemini against the same answering pipeline with the gate. Track:

- **Answer coverage:** answered questions / all questions.
- **Error rate among answers:** incorrect answers / answered questions.
- **Unsupported-answer rate:** factual answers given without adequate evidence.
- **Unnecessary abstention:** answerable questions left unanswered.
- Latency and API cost.

Keep development examples separate from the final comparison, including alternate versions of the same drawing. The gate earns its place if it reduces unsupported answers without sacrificing too much useful coverage. That is the narrow experiment we need before adding more checks.
